restatements.text: Provides the title of the Act.
Lists findings and declarations regarding taxation, cost of living, and retirement savings in California.
States the purpose of the Act is to protect personal property from new taxes and require taxes to apply prospectively.
Adds Article VIII to the California Constitution.

Prohibits the state from enacting or collecting a tax on the ownership or control of personal savings, retirement holdings, and assets after January 1, 2026, while exempting existing taxes and real property taxes.

Prohibits retroactive taxes that result in liability based on past conduct, activities, or residency status, with exceptions for limited retroactivity during declared emergencies or fiscal emergencies.
Defines "retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other forms of personal savings" and "tax".
Applies the article to all statewide initiatives submitted on or after January 1, 2026.
Declares that this measure conflicts with and overrides any other initiative on the same ballot that imposes taxes on personal savings or enacts retroactive taxes.
Sets the effective and operative dates of the Act.
Requires the Act to be liberally construed to give effect to its purposes.
Requires the Attorney General to appoint independent counsel if state officials refuse to defend the Act, and provides a continuous appropriation from the General Fund to cover the costs.

evidence.quote: No state law and no provision of this Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026 may enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other forms of personal savings, whether held directly or indirectly.
evidence.why: It removes the government's power to levy taxes on the ownership of personal property, assets, and retirement accounts.

evidence.quote: No state law and no provision of this Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026 may enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax that operates retroactively to result in tax liability based on conduct, activities, or a status that occurred or was present prior to the effective date
evidence.why: It restricts the government's authority to enact retroactive tax liabilities.

evidence.why: It protects individuals' retirement security by preventing the state from taxing the ownership of retirement holdings.

evidence.quote: "Retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other forms of personal savings" means pensions; retirement accounts including but not limited to 401 (k) accounts, 403(b) accounts, and all other individual retirement accounts
evidence.why: It explicitly ensures that pensions and retirement accounts are protected from new ownership taxes.

evidence.quote: No state law and no provision of this Constitution enacted on or after January 1, 2026 may enact, create, impose, or authorize collection of a tax on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other forms of personal savings
evidence.why: It prohibits the state from imposing new taxes on the ownership of personal property, which is defined to include business assets.

evidence.why: It guarantees continuous, unrestricted funding from the General Fund for the specific purpose of paying independent counsel to defend the measure in court.

analysis.answer: Current law was not provided. The measure amends the California Constitution to prohibit the state from imposing taxes on the ownership or control of personal property, including retirement accounts, pensions, business interests, and financial assets, after January 1, 2026. It also bans retroactive taxes based on past conduct or residency, with limited exceptions for brief retroactivity during declared emergencies.

Direct costs include continuous appropriations from the General Fund to pay for independent counsel if the measure is challenged and state officials decline to defend it. Opportunity costs include the foregone ability of the state to raise revenue through wealth taxes or asset taxes to fund state programs.

Individuals and families with retirement savings, pensions, business interests, and financial assets benefit by being protected from potential ownership or wealth taxes. High-net-worth individuals may disproportionately benefit since wealth taxes typically target accumulated assets. The costs are borne by the state government, which loses the option to implement such taxes, and potentially by residents who rely on public services if revenue needs cannot be met.

Legislators may respond to the restriction on taxing personal property by seeking revenue through increased income, sales, or real property taxes. Wealthy individuals and businesses may be more inclined to keep their assets and residency in the state, knowing they are constitutionally protected from wealth or retroactive taxes.

The text asserts the problem of an affordability crisis, high tax burdens, and potential future taxes on retirement savings and personal assets. The mechanism (a constitutional ban) effectively prevents the state from enacting a wealth tax or taxing retirement accounts.

Current and future owners of retirement accounts, business interests, and financial assets gain protection from taxation. The Attorney General loses prosecutorial discretion over whether to defend the measure, and the power to defend it is shifted to an independent counsel.

The economic effect of wealth taxes (and banning them) is disputed. Some economists argue wealth taxes deter investment and prompt capital flight, while others argue they are necessary to reduce inequality and fund essential services without significantly harming economic growth. The impact of banning retroactive taxes on state fiscal stability is also debated.
Enforcement costs would primarily arise from potential litigation over the measure, for which the text mandates an open-ended continuous appropriation to retain independent counsel.
Because it amends the California Constitution, it can only be undone by another voter-approved constitutional amendment.

flags.quote: "Retirement holdings, individually-owned assets, and other forms of personal savings" means pensions; retirement accounts including but not limited to 401 (k) accounts, 403(b) accounts, and all other individual retirement accounts; mutual funds; and all personal property, whether tangible or intangible, including but not limited to financial assets, investment accounts, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property, personal belongings, and other assets used to produce or collect income or savings for retirement or financial planning.
flags.note: The definition expansively includes "all personal property", "business interests", and "intellectual property", going far beyond typical retirement holdings.

flags.quote: (a) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 12500) of Part 2 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code or any other law, the Attorney General shall appoint independent counsel
flags.note: Explicit override of existing laws regarding the Attorney General's duties.

flags.quote: Section 6. Severability. The provisions of this Act are severable.
This Act shall take effect at the earliest possible date in accordance with Section 10 of Article II of the California Constitution. This Act shall become operative on the same day it takes effect.
flags.note: Specifies the effective and operative dates.

flags.quote: ...prohibiting the imposition of new taxes on our personal property... as well as requiring all new taxes to only apply prospectively.
flags.note: The measure bundles a ban on taxing personal property with a ban on retroactive taxes.
